articles.title: 18 Types of Game Testing Techniques (With Examples & Tools)
articles.excerpt: Games are a huge business. Newzoo's 2026 forecast puts global games revenue at about $213.9 billion, up 6.1% from the year before, with roughly 3.7 billion players worldwide. Mobile alone brings in ar…
articles.body: Games are a huge business. Newzoo's 2026 forecast puts global games revenue at about $213.9 billion, up 6.1% from the year before, with roughly 3.7 billion players worldwide. Mobile alone brings in around 57% of that money, or $121.1 billion. Growth is slowing, though, and it's moving from new downloads to keeping players around and getting them to spend. That puts pressure on quality. A game that crashes on a popular phone, lags in a match, or breaks a purchase flow loses players fast, and they rarely come back. Testing is how studios catch those problems before players do. But "game testing" isn't one activity. It's a set of techniques, each built to find a different kind of problem.

articles.title: brick.blue: An Exchange Where AI Agents Trade Tokens for Money
articles.excerpt: I run a paid API gateway (x402.freeq.one) — about 32 tools agents can call, settled in USDC on Base. The supply side was never my problem. The missing piece was the demand side: a place where agents a…
articles.body: I run a paid API gateway (x402.freeq.one) — about 32 tools agents can call, settled in USDC on Base. The supply side was never my problem. The missing piece was the demand side: a place where agents actually hold money and spend it. Last week I found brick.blue , and it's the closest thing to that market I've seen. The market that didn't exist brick.blue frames the AI economy in three phases: Energy → Compute. Power and silicon become machine time. Utilities and fabs win. Compute → Tokens. Machine time becomes inference. Model providers win. Tokens → Value. Inference becomes something somebody pays for. No exchange existed for this — and it's the only phase an agent can enter directly, because the agent's ability to think, call tools, and act is the input rather than the product.

articles.title: Turning what you read into Anki cards without the typing
articles.excerpt: Turning what you read into Anki cards without the typing Here's a workflow that fails quietly, every day, for a lot of people: You read something good — a paper, a lecture PDF, a long article, a YouTu…
articles.body: Turning what you read into Anki cards without the typing Here's a workflow that fails quietly, every day, for a lot of people: You read something good — a paper, a lecture PDF, a long article, a YouTube lecture. You think "this belongs in Anki." You open Anki, create a deck, and start typing cards by hand. You make six cards, it's been twenty minutes, and you close the window. The material never makes it in. Not because spaced repetition doesn't work — it obviously does — but because the input step is manual while the review step is automated. Anki's scheduler is a piece of software. Your card creation is you, typing. The bottleneck is card creation, not review Most "I fell off Anki" stories I've heard are really "I stopped making cards" stories.

articles.title: Migrating an Application to the Cloud Without Downtime: Cutover Plan
articles.excerpt: Most products can move to the cloud without downtime. To do it, you need to settle four things before the cutover weekend: how the database moves, when DNS changes, how long the old and new environmen…
articles.body: Most products can move to the cloud without downtime. To do it, you need to settle four things before the cutover weekend: how the database moves, when DNS changes, how long the old and new environments run together, and what exact signal makes you roll back. When a migration causes an outage, the cause is usually one of those four decisions being skipped. The cloud provider is rarely the problem. If you are a CTO or technical founder, the new environment is probably already running. Staging works and the load test passed. Still, you are worried about Saturday night. What happens to the orders, sign-ups and payments that arrive during the switch? You are right to worry. Why does downtime happen when everything was tested? The new servers are rarely what fails during a migration.

articles.title: My Mutation Check Stopped Because a Scheduled Task Wrote a Ledger
articles.excerpt: A field note from the autonomous Claude Code agent I run every day on one Windows PC. The numbers come from its own ledgers, not from memory. Free to read first: a PDF sample of the book behind this s…
articles.body: A field note from the autonomous Claude Code agent I run every day on one Windows PC. The numbers come from its own ledgers, not from memory. Free to read first: a PDF sample of the book behind this setup — its first 3 chapters: https://dbsoul.gumroad.com/l/autonomous-ai-agents-claude-code-free-sample My agent checks its tests with mutation testing. It changes one line of the real code, runs the tests, and expects at least one test to fail. A mutant that no test catches means a test is missing. The mutants run in a copy of the repository, not in the real one. There is one more guard. Before and after each mutant, the check records the modification time and size of the files in the real data folder, where the ledgers live. If anything there changed, it stops and prints which files changed.

articles.body: SpaceX just broke an uncharacteristically long Starlink launch drought. The company sent 27 of its Starlink internet satellites to low Earth orbit (LEO) today (Oct. 12), launching them atop a Falcon 9 rocket from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base at 8:28 p.m. EDT (5:28 p.m. local time; 0028 GMT on Oct. 13) It was the first Starlink mission for a Falcon 9 since Sept. 19 , which was another 27-satellite liftoff from Vandenberg. For some perspective on this recent gap: Between Aug. 19 and Sept. 6, a span of 19 days, SpaceX launched seven Starlink missions with Falcon 9s. The Falcon 9's first stage rests on the deck of a ship at sea shortly after the Oct. 12 launch. articles.title: NASA’s SpaceX CRS-35 Mission to Launch Health Research
articles.excerpt: NASA experiments focused on human and plant health and drug-resistant organisms will travel to the International Space Station aboard SpaceX’s 35th Commercial Resupply Services mission for the agency…
articles.body: NASA experiments focused on human and plant health and drug-resistant organisms will travel to the International Space Station aboard SpaceX’s 35th Commercial Resupply Services mission for the agency from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, advancing research that benefits life on Earth and future exploration. This research supports astronaut health during long-duration missions through four investigations from the agency’s Biological and Physical Sciences division, including 3D models of the human brain, a crop disease study, a faster way to assess astronaut health, and an analysis of antibiotic-resistant bacteria aboard the space station.

articles.title: The 'Halloween Fireballs' are coming. Here's what to expect from the Taurids this year
articles.excerpt: The Southern and Northern Taurid meteor showers will produce occasional bright, slow-moving meteors worldwide during October and November, with moon-free peaks in 2026.
articles.body: They don't produce anything like the torrent of "shooting stars" associated with August's Perseids or December's Geminids, but the Taurid meteor showers have something else going for them — fireballs. The Taurids are famous for occasionally producing exceptionally bright, slow-moving meteors that can streak dramatically across the night sky from September to December. As a bonus, they're visible from both the Northern and Southern hemispheres. That's because they appear to emanate from the constellation Taurus, which sits close to the ecliptic, the apparent path the sun takes across the sky as Earth orbits around it. The Taurids are actually two closely related showers — the Southern Taurids and Northern Taurids — whose activity overlaps in late October and November.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 12, 1964: The Soviet Union launches Voskhod 1, the 1st multi-person cosmonaut crew, into space
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 12, 1964, the Soviet Union launched Voskhod 1, a 24-hour crewed mission that achieved several "firsts" for human spaceflight. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 12, 1964, the Soviet Union launched Voskhod 1, a 24-hour crewed mission that achieved several "firsts" for human spaceflight . This was the first time that a spacecraft carried more than one person into orbit, with three cosmonauts packed inside the spacecraft. Only two cosmonauts were originally supposed to fly on this mission, but Soviet politicians pressured the Russian space program to add one more. This left no room for spacesuits on board, so this also became the first spaceflight without spacesuits . Two of the crewmembers, an engineer and a doctor, became the first civilians to go to space. On Oct. 12, 1964, the Soviet Union launched the first multiperson mission, Voskhod 1, which launched three Russian cosmonauts into space.
